_schema: PRD FR-7. Hand-authored. Never generated -- the firewall (FR-5) serves from here or says 'not yet documented'.

_fields.id: stable key, also the FSRS item id for grammar-kind items
_fields.en: the explanation shown to the user
_fields.hindi_contrast: OPTIONAL. Present only where the analogy genuinely holds.
_fields.interference_warning: true where Hindi intuition actively misleads

entries.en: は marks the topic — what the sentence is about, often already known. が marks the subject as new, identified, or the answer to a question.
examples: 私は学生です。 (As for me, I'm a student.)
誰が来ましたか。 (Who came?) — answer: 田中さんが来ました。
entries.hindi_contrast: は is closer to तो in 'मैं तो छात्र हूँ'. NOT ने — ने is ergative and marks the agent of a completed transitive verb, which Japanese does not do at all.

entries.en: は marks a topic in contrast to others. も replaces it to mean 'also' or 'too' — it never stacks with は.
examples: 私は行きます。 (I'm going.)
私も行きます。 (I'm going too.)
entries.hindi_contrast: も corresponds closely to भी. 'मैं भी जाऊँगा' is exactly 私も行きます.

entries.en: を marks the direct object of a transitive verb.
examples: ご飯を食べます。 (I eat rice.)
水を飲みます。 (I drink water.)
entries.hindi_contrast: Roughly को on a definite object, but Japanese を is required on any direct object, definite or not.

entries.en: に marks a destination, a point in time, or where something exists. で marks where an action happens, or the means used.
examples: 駅に行きます。 (I go to the station.)
駅で待ちます。 (I wait at the station.)
電車で行きます。 (I go by train.)
entries.hindi_contrast: Both often surface as में/पर in Hindi, which is exactly why the に/で split is hard — Hindi does not force the existence-vs-action distinction.

entries.en: Japanese pairs verbs: a transitive one (something does it, takes を) and an intransitive one (it happens, takes が). They are different words, not a voice change.
examples: ドアを開けます。 (I open the door.) — transitive 開ける
ドアが開きます。 (The door opens.) — intransitive 開く
entries.hindi_contrast: Hindi has the same pattern — खोलना vs खुलना. This one transfers well; trust the instinct.

entries.en: The て-form links clauses ('and then'), requests with ください, and forms the progressive with いる. It carries no tense of its own — the final verb sets the tense.
examples: 起きて、食べます。 (I get up and eat.)
待ってください。 (Please wait.)
食べています。 (I am eating.)
entries.hindi_contrast: Close to the कर conjunctive: 'उठकर खाता हूँ'. The tenseless-linker behaviour matches well.

entries.en: です/ます is the polite register; plain form (だ, 食べる) is casual. Pick one per conversation. Plain form is still required inside subordinate clauses even when speaking politely.
examples: 食べます。 (polite)
食べる。 (plain)
食べる時、水を飲みます。 (plain inside the clause, polite at the end — correct)
entries.hindi_contrast: Comparable to आप/तुम/तू levels, but Japanese marks it on the VERB rather than the pronoun, and dropping the pronoun does not drop the register.

entries.en: Counting requires a counter matched to the thing counted. 一つ/二つ is the general one for objects; 人 for people, 枚 for flat things, 本 for long things.
examples: コーヒーを一つください。 (One coffee, please.)
二人です。 (Two people.)
entries.hindi_contrast: Hindi counts bare — 'दो लोग'. Japanese never does; a bare number before a noun is ungrammatical.

entries.en: い-adjectives conjugate themselves (高い → 高くない). な-adjectives take な before a noun and conjugate with です/じゃない (好き → 好きじゃない).
examples: 高い店 (an expensive shop)
好きな店 (a shop I like)
高くないです。 (It isn't expensive.)

entries.en: か at the end makes a question. Word order does not change, and no rising intonation is required in polite speech.
examples: 行きます。 (I go.)
行きますか。 (Do you go?)
entries.hindi_contrast: Like क्या, but placed at the END rather than the start.

entries.en: ます becomes ません for polite negation. です becomes じゃないです or ではありません.
examples: 食べます → 食べません
学生です → 学生じゃないです

entries.en: ます becomes ました for polite past. です becomes でした.
examples: 食べます → 食べました
高いです → 高かったです (note: the ADJECTIVE takes the past, not です)

entries.en: の links nouns, most often showing possession or attribute. The modifier comes first.
examples: 私の本 (my book)
日本語の先生 (a Japanese-language teacher)
entries.hindi_contrast: Like का/की/के but INVARIANT — の never agrees with gender or number.

entries.en: ある for inanimate things, いる for animate ones. The distinction is grammatical, not optional.
examples: 店があります。 (There is a shop.)
友達がいます。 (I have a friend / a friend is there.)
entries.hindi_contrast: Hindi uses है for both. There is no Hindi cue for this split.

entries.en: Japanese is subject–object–verb, and the verb must come last. Other elements move freely because particles, not position, mark their roles.
examples: 私はご飯を食べます。 (I rice eat.)
entries.hindi_contrast: Identical to Hindi SOV — 'मैं खाना खाता हूँ'. This is the single largest free transfer available.

entries.en: Subjects and objects are dropped whenever context supplies them. Repeating 私は sounds unnatural.
examples: 食べましたか。 (Did [you] eat?)
はい、食べました。 (Yes, [I] ate.)
entries.hindi_contrast: Hindi drops pronouns too, but its verb still agrees for person and gender. Japanese verbs carry NO agreement, so the only recovery is context.

entries.en: Noun + をください asks for a thing. て-form + ください asks for an action.
examples: 水をください。 (Water, please.)
待ってください。 (Please wait.)

entries.en: て-form + もいいですか asks permission.
examples: 写真を撮ってもいいですか。 (May I take a photo?)

entries.en: と joins nouns exhaustively ('and', a complete list). や implies the list is partial.
examples: 肉と魚 (meat and fish — just those)
肉や魚 (meat, fish, and so on)
entries.hindi_contrast: と is और for a closed list. Hindi has no common equivalent of や's 'and such'.

entries.en: Japanese distinguishes words by PITCH pattern across morae, not by stress. 箸 (chopsticks, HL) and 橋 (bridge, LH) differ only in pitch.
examples: はし HL = chopsticks
はし LH = bridge
entries.hindi_contrast: Hindi uses weight-based STRESS — a heavy syllable is said louder and longer. Applying that to Japanese produces the single most persistent foreign-accent marker. Pitch is a melody, not emphasis.
entries.source: PRD FR-6; NHK 日本語発音アクセント辞典
